arguments.text: Everyone wants safe, reliable Muni. The question is whether a 15-year tax with no strings attached will deliver it. The Yes campaign warns of devastating service cuts if Prop H fails. But that dodges the real question: Why guarantee SFMTA a new tax revenue stream without requiring it to meet a single efficiency or performance target? Supporters boast that Muni has eliminated vacant positions, trimmed management and found $137 million in annual savings. Great. That proves reform is possible. Prop H should require more reform, not guarantee new revenue regardless of results. They also promise “strong oversight and independent audits.” But oversight is not accountability. Prop H requires an efficiency review, but does not require SFMTA to implement its recommendations. There are no binding efficiency targets, performance benchmarks, or requirements that future tax dollars depend on results. And who pays? Prop H taxes property based on square footage, not value. A modest home can owe nearly the same tax as a far more valuable home of similar size. Renters aren’t spared, either, since landlords can pass through part of the tax. Muni is too important to keep funding the same way and hoping for different results. Before approving a 15-year tax, voters must demand binding reforms, measurable performance standards, and real accountability. Vote NO on Prop H.

arguments.text: San Franciscans are being asked to fund Muni’s $300 million deficit for 15 years with no strings attached. False threats. Nobody wants longer wait times or service cuts, but a new tax isn’t the only option. Nothing in this proposition requires SFMTA to cut costs, hit efficiency targets, or act on a spending review as a condition of receiving this money. No sunset tied to results. The tax runs through 2042 regardless of whether ridership, fares, or costs ever normalize. A toothless review, collected after the money’s already in hand. The measure calls for an “efficiency review,” but not until April 2028, nine months after the tax kicks in. Even then, the review only has to report its findings to SFMTA’s own board. Nothing requires the agency to act on a single recommendation, and nothing ties future funding to whether it does. A flat tax, not a fair one. The tax is based on square footage, not property value. A modest home and a far more valuable one of similar size nearby will pay nearly the same amount. Renters aren’t spared either, since landlords can pass through the tax increase to tenants. A 15-year tax with no results-based sunset, no binding reforms, and no independent check on whether the money is spent well isn’t the accountability that SFMTA needs. It’s a blank check. Vote No on H.

arguments.text: Trump’s Federal spending cuts have devastated transportation systems across the country. Given these cuts and the loss of other funding, Muni faces 30% service cuts and the elimination of at least 20 bus routes. That’s just a fact. Mayor Lurie has taken bold action to make Muni more efficient BEFORE ever proposing H for the ballot. With new leadership, the agency eliminated 500 vacant positions, cut management, and froze non-operator hiring, saving $140 million. Muni doubled fare inspectors and reduced fare evasion by 30%. Wait times and reliability have improved, and Muni’s favorability is at an all time high. The tax isn’t flat. The San Francisco Republican Party is wrong. H is the first fair, tiered parcel tax in San Francisco history. 95% of homeowners pay the lowest amount. Large commercial buildings and mansions pay the most. 70% of the revenue comes from the city’s largest properties. Rent-controlled units are protected and won’t pay more than $65 a year. Strong oversight. H requires independent audits and mandates citizen oversight for the life of the tax. And not one penny can be spent on anything other than Muni operations. World-class public transportation requires investment. “Investing in Muni is just smart economics. The economic activity Muni generates funds emergency response, parks, and libraries.” - Former Controller Ben Rosenfield. We owe it to the next generation of San Franciscans to make sure that Muni remains the system we all love. Vote Yes on H.

arguments.heading: Save Muni. Protect San Francisco’s Future.
arguments.text: Muni carries more than 520,000 riders every weekday — seniors, students, workers, and people with disabilities who depend on reliable transit. Without new revenue, Muni faces a $307 million deficit by 2027, growing to $398 million by 2030, meaning up to 20 routes eliminated and service cut in half. For more than a century, SPUR has championed public transit as essential to San Francisco’s success, from early advocacy for the Municipal Railway itself through decades of ballot campaigns to keep Muni funded, reliable, and accountable. This measure continues that legacy. It raises roughly $177 million a year through a fair, tiered parcel tax. Ninety‑five percent of single‑family homeowners pay just $129 a year. Rent‑controlled tenants pay no more than $65 a year, and landlords cannot pass on more. Seniors are exempt on their primary homes; larger properties pay proportionally more. Muni has earned this investment, already saving $250 million since 2019 through efficiency improvements, with rider satisfaction at a decades‑high 78%. This measure funds operations only — the buses and trains San Franciscans rely on every day. This measure has broad, unified support from the Mayor, the Board of Supervisors, labor, business, and transit and housing advocates alike, with no formal opposition. Combined with the regional Connect Bay Area measure, it’s the difference between a Muni that works and a Muni in crisis. Vote YES.

arguments.text: Muni is an absolutely essential service for San Francisco’s working class and powered by the working class. In one of the wealthiest cities in the country, flooded with billions of dollars of investment into companies whose employees depend on public transit, it is shameful that the rich won’t pay their fair share and are placing our transit system in jeopardy. A popular proposal, 2024’s Prop L, would have preserved Muni funding by requiring ride‑hail companies like Uber, Lyft and Waymo to redistribute a small portion of their earnings to keep buses running in a city that has allowed them to thrive. Fifty‑six percent of San Francisco voters approved, but it wasn’t enough to overcome a well‑funded corporate lobbying campaign and backroom deals at City Hall. They put us in this position. DSA SF believes a better world is possible and a better way of funding transit is necessary. We were part of the coalition which overcame corporate opposition to ensure the Stronger Muni for All measure is a progressive parcel tax. We secured changes to the tax so that downtown landlords pay closer to their fair share, local unions remain strong, and working people pay less. But we are nowhere near the finish line. We recommend San Franciscans vote yes on this measure. DSA SF stands in solidarity with Muni operators and riders by keeping Muni running and resolving the current funding emergency, but small and reactive reforms like these can’t deliver the affordable, expansive, and financially sustainable public transit system that San Francisco’s working class deserves. For that, we need to think bigger, and we need to win working class power in order to bring those ideas to life. Join us and get organized.

arguments.text: Public transit is climate action. Every rider on a Muni bus or train means lower emissions, less congestion, cleaner air. If San Francisco is serious about its climate goals, we cannot let our transit system collapse. Transit cuts set back years of climate progress. Sustainable growth depends on reliable transit. Prop H keeps San Francisco’s buses and trains running so people can choose transit over cars — protecting our climate goals and our quality of life. Vote Yes on H for a cleaner, more sustainable San Francisco.

arguments.heading: SENIORS AND PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES URGE SUPPORT FOR MUNI AND PROP H.
arguments.text: For seniors and people with disabilities, Muni isn’t a convenience — it’s independence. It’s the ride to a doctor’s appointment, the trip to the pharmacy, the way to see friends and stay connected to community. For those who don’t or can’t drive, Muni is often the only way to get around the city we call home. Without Prop H, Muni service will be cut and accessible transit options will shrink even further for the people who depend on them most. Isolation is one of the greatest threats facing seniors and people with disabilities. Reliable transit prevents it. Don’t let service cuts cut us off from our city. Vote Yes on H.

arguments.heading: BUSINESS LEADERS SUPPORT PROP H TO DRIVE OUR ECONOMIC RECOVERY
arguments.text: San Francisco’s economy runs on Muni. Forty percent of San Franciscans who work downtown ride Muni to their jobs, and small businesses across the city depend on customers, employees, and deliveries moving reliably through our streets. A weaker Muni means a weaker economy — for big employers and corner stores alike. Prop H protects the transit service our commercial corridors depend on, and it comes with real accountability. Independent audits ensure every dollar funds Muni service directly and can never be redirected. Muni has already demonstrated fiscal discipline, eliminating vacant positions and saving $137 million in personnel costs. From neighborhood merchants to major employers, San Francisco’s business community knows that a functioning transit system is essential to a functioning economy. Investing in Muni is investing in our recovery. Vote Yes on H for a stronger economy and a stronger Muni.

arguments.text: San Francisco Democrats have always fought for a city that works for everyone. A transit system every resident can rely on is a critical part of that vision. Muni is core to the kind of affordable, equitable city we believe in. Prop H protects Muni service with a fair, tiered tax where those that can afford to pay more will. And it has accountability built in with independent audits ensuring every dollar goes directly to Muni service. Investing in public transit is investing in climate action, economic opportunity, and equity for every neighborhood in San Francisco. Democratic clubs across the city are united behind Prop H because a stronger Muni means a stronger, fairer San Francisco.

arguments.heading: VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION H
arguments.text: We support Muni. We want safe, reliable public transportation. But another long‑term parcel tax is not the solution to SFMTA’s financial problems. Proposition H would create a 15‑year parcel tax, beginning in 2027, with rates adjusted annually for inflation. According to SFMTA, approximately $150 million each year would go toward reducing its existing deficit, while about $10 million would support service‑quality improvements. That raises an important question: If this new tax does not solve SFMTA’s underlying structural deficit, what happens when the next funding gap comes? San Francisco homeowners, property owners, small businesses, working families, and renters are already struggling with one of the highest costs of living and doing business in the country. Another long‑term tax adds more financial pressure to our city. Before asking San Franciscans to pay more for the next 15 years, SFMTA should demonstrate fiscal responsibility, measurable results, transparency, and sustainable solutions to its operational and financial problems. We support Muni. But supporting Muni does not mean automatically supporting another tax. Fix the underlying problems before asking San Franciscans to pay more. VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION H.

proposal.value: Starting July 1, 2027, and continuing until June 30, 2042, Proposition H would fund Muni service through a new annual parcel tax on real estate in San Francisco. The tax would be adjusted annually for inflation. The proposed 2027 tax rates would be: • Single-Family Residential Parcels: • A base tax of $129. • For buildings with more than 3,000 square feet of building area: • $0.42 per square foot between 3,001 and 5,000, and • $1.99 per square foot over 5,000. • Multifamily Residential Parcels: • A base tax of $249. • For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area: • $0.195 per square foot over 5,000. • This tax is capped at $50,000 per parcel. • Non-Residential Parcels: • A base tax of $799. • For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area: • $0.76 per square foot between 5,001 and 50,000, • $0.84 per square foot between 50,001 and 250,000, and • $0.99 per square foot over 250,000. • This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel. • Mixed-Use Parcels: • A base tax of $799. • For buildings with more than 5,000 square feet of building area: • A combination of the marginal rates for residential and non-residential parcels above. • This tax is capped at $400,000 per parcel. • Parcels with No Buildings: • No base tax. • $392 for land area over 2,000 square feet. The tax would not apply to: 1. Properties or portions of properties not required to pay standard property taxes; and 2. Single Room Occupancy (SRO) units and their shared facilities such as kitchens or bathrooms. Most homeowners aged 65 or older living in their primary home would get a discount or pay no tax. Revenues from the tax would only be used for Muni service and administering the tax. In addition to the annual required audit by an independent auditor, an annual report and efficiency review would be required. This measure would increase the City’s spending limit for four years. Owners could pass up to 50% of the tax onto tenants in rent-controlled units where the rent was set before June 1, 2027, up to a maximum of $65 per unit per year.

way_it_is_now.value: The Municipal Railway (Muni) provides public transit in San Francisco, including bus, light rail, streetcar, and cable car. Muni provides over 500,000 rides per weekday. Muni service is funded by transit fares and local, state and federal sources, but not through a parcel tax. State law limits the total revenue, including tax revenue, that the City may spend each year. The voters may approve increases to this limit for up to four years. Owners of rent-controlled residential property in the City are generally limited in what costs they can pass onto their tenants.
